concept.name: Exchange-traded note
concept.definition: An unsecured, senior debt obligation of a financial institution that trades on a national securities exchange and whose payment terms are linked to the performance of a reference index or benchmark. Unlike an ETF, an ETN holds no underlying assets, so investors bear the issuer's credit risk, and ETNs can result in the loss of the entire investment.
concept.intuition: An ETN is essentially a promise from a bank to pay you the return of an index. You get index-linked payoff with bond-like exposure to the bank's solvency.
concept.mechanics: The issuer commits to pay at maturity (or on early redemption) an amount based on the reference index level, minus fees; an intraday indicative value is published. ETNs trade on exchanges like stocks, but their market price can deviate from indicative value, and issuers may call, accelerate, or suspend new issuance, which can drive prices to large premia.
concept.failure_modes: Issuer default or downgrade reduces the ETN's value regardless of index performance — ETN holders are unsecured creditors. Suspension of issuance can decouple price from indicative value, and maturity calls or delistings can force realization at inopportune times, as seen in volatility-linked ETN collapses.
concept.misconceptions: That ETNs own the underlying assets like ETFs — they are pure credit exposure plus an index-linked payoff formula. Also, 'exchange-traded' does not imply investment-company protections; ETNs are not registered under the Investment Company Act.
concept.example: An ETN linked to a commodity index drops in price when the issuing bank's credit spreads widen, even on a day the index itself is unchanged.
